# Amazon VPC: questions

## Worked examples

<!-- quiz:start id=vpc-q004 -->
### Question 1

A company runs data-processing workers on Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets of a VPC. Each night the workers upload several terabytes of result files to an Amazon S3 bucket in the same AWS Region. All outbound traffic from the private subnets goes through a NAT gateway, and the monthly bill shows high NAT gateway data processing charges. The workers must still download software updates from the internet. The uploads must reach Amazon S3 privately. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?

- Create an interface endpoint for Amazon S3 in each private subnet, and send the uploads to the DNS name of the interface endpoint.
- Move the workers to public subnets, assign a public IPv4 address to each worker, and send all traffic through the internet gateway.
- Create a gateway endpoint for Amazon S3, and associate the endpoint with the route tables of the private subnets that the workers use.
- Create a NAT gateway in each Availability Zone, and point the route table of each private subnet to the NAT gateway in its zone.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create a gateway endpoint for Amazon S3, and associate the endpoint with the route tables of the private subnets that the workers use.

**Deciding phrases.** "upload several terabytes of result files to an Amazon S3 bucket in the same AWS Region", "NAT gateway data processing charges", "must still download software updates from the internet", "MOST cost-effective"

**Think aloud.**

1. I read the last sentence first: it asks for the MOST cost-effective way to meet every requirement.
2. I mark the constraints: the bucket is in the same Region, the NAT gateway data processing charge is the problem, the workers still need the internet for updates, and the uploads stay private.
3. Before I look at the options, I predict a gateway endpoint for Amazon S3, because a gateway endpoint has no hourly or data processing charge and keeps the traffic off the NAT gateway.
4. I remove the public subnets, because the uploads must stay private and every public IPv4 address is billed. I remove a NAT gateway in each zone, because each NAT gateway still charges for every gigabyte it processes.
5. Between the gateway endpoint and the interface endpoint the difference is the price; both keep the traffic private, but the interface endpoint charges per hour in each zone and per GB, and the stem asks for the lowest cost, so the gateway endpoint wins.
6. Check: the gateway endpoint carries the uploads privately, the NAT gateway still serves the updates, and no new hourly charge appears. Time: 90 seconds.

**Why.** The expensive bytes are the uploads to Amazon S3. [Gateway VPC endpoints provide reliable connectivity to Amazon S3 and DynamoDB without requiring an internet gateway or a NAT device for your VPC](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-gateway-endpoint-s3-dynamodb-no-privatelink), and [There are no data processing or hourly charges for using Gateway Type VPC endpoints](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-gateway-endpoint-no-hourly-or-processing-charge). The default route to the NAT gateway stays, so the software updates still work.

**Why not.**

- "Create an interface endpoint for Amazon S3 in ...": It works and stays private, but an interface endpoint is [billed for each hour that your interface VPC endpoint is provisioned in each Availability Zone](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-interface-endpoint-billed-hour-per-az-and-gb) and per GB processed.
- "Move the workers to public subnets, assign a ...": The uploads would leave the private subnets, which breaks the private requirement, and [AWS charges for all public IPv4 addresses](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-public-ipv4-charge-2024).
- "Create a NAT gateway in each Availability Zone, ...": Each NAT gateway still charges for [each gigabyte of data that it processes](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-pricing-dimensions), so the upload bytes are still billed for processing.

**Twin.** If the stem said "servers in the data center upload the files" instead: an interface endpoint, because S3 [gateway endpoints do not allow access from on-premises networks, from peered VPCs in other AWS Regions, or through a transit gateway](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-gateway-endpoint-no-onprem-cross-region-tgw).

**Takeaway.** Send same-Region Amazon S3 traffic through a gateway endpoint, not through a NAT gateway.

**Review.** [A NAT gateway lets private instances start connections and charges hourly and per gigabyte](2-deep.md#a-nat-gateway-lets-private-instances-start-connections-and-charges-hourly-and-per-gigabyte-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 2

A company runs a reporting service on Amazon EC2 instances in a private subnet. Amazon Linux instances in another subnet of the same VPC call the service on TCP 8443, and every call times out. The client subnet uses the default network ACL. The security group of the service allows inbound TCP 8443 from the security group of the clients. A VPC flow log for the service shows an ACCEPT record for each request and a REJECT record for each response. The company must restore the calls. Which change will meet these requirements in the MOST secure way?

- Add an outbound rule to the security group of the service instances that allows TCP ports 32768-61000 to the security group of the clients.
- Add an outbound rule to the network ACL of the service subnet that allows TCP ports 32768-61000 to the CIDR block of the client subnet.
- Replace the outbound rules of the network ACL of the service subnet with one rule that allows all traffic to every destination.
- Add an inbound rule to the network ACL of the client subnet that allows TCP ports 32768-61000 from the CIDR block of the service subnet.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Add an outbound rule to the network ACL of the service subnet that allows TCP ports 32768-61000 to the CIDR block of the client subnet.

**Deciding phrases.** "Amazon Linux instances", "ACCEPT record for each request and a REJECT record for each response", "MOST secure"

**Think aloud.**

1. I read the last sentence first: it asks for the change that restores the calls in the MOST secure way.
2. I mark the constraints: the clients run Amazon Linux, the client subnet uses the default network ACL, the security group of the service allows the requests, and the flow log shows an ACCEPT for each request and a REJECT for each response.
3. Before I look at the options, I predict an outbound security group rule on the service instances for the reply ports, because the responses are the traffic that fails.
4. I remove the inbound rule on the client network ACL, because the default network ACL allows all inbound and outbound traffic. I remove the rule that allows all outbound traffic, because it opens every port to every destination.
5. Between the outbound security group rule and the outbound network ACL rule, the difference is state. My first idea breaks because security groups are stateful, so the security group already lets the responses out and only the stateless network ACL drops them. I choose the outbound network ACL rule for ports 32768-61000 to the client subnet.
6. Check: the requests already pass, the new rule lets out only the replies to the client subnet, and nothing else opens. Time: 120 seconds.

**Why.** AWS shows the same record pair for a ping: [A REJECT record for the response ping that the network ACL denied](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-flow-logs-diagnose-stateless-nacl). The request passes, and the response is dropped on its way out, because [network ACLs perform stateless filtering](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-faq-stateful-vs-stateless). The service subnet needs an outbound rule for the reply ports that the Amazon Linux clients use.

**Why not.**

- "Add an outbound rule to the security group ...": Because [security groups are stateful](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-sg-connection-tracking-stateful), the security group already lets the responses out; the network ACL drops them.
- "Replace the outbound rules of the network ACL ...": It works, but it opens every port to every destination, which is far less secure than one rule for the reply ports of the client subnet.
- "Add an inbound rule to the network ACL ...": The client subnet uses the default network ACL, and [The default network ACL allows all inbound and outbound traffic](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-nacl-every-subnet-associated), so the responses pass there.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the flow log shows a REJECT record for each request" instead: fix the inbound side, because the request itself is blocked before the service can answer.

**Takeaway.** An ACCEPT for the request and a REJECT for the response point to an outbound network ACL rule.

**Review.** [Flow logs record accepted and rejected traffic so they show where packets drop](2-deep.md#flow-logs-record-accepted-and-rejected-traffic-so-they-show-where-packets-drop-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 3

A company is designing a VPC for an internet-facing web application. The application has an Application Load Balancer, a fleet of Amazon EC2 application instances, and a database that runs on Amazon EC2 instances. The application must keep running if one Availability Zone fails. The application instances and the database must have no direct network path to or from the internet. Which subnet layout will meet these requirements?

- Place the load balancer, the application instances and the database instances in public subnets in two Availability Zones, and restrict access with security groups.
- Place the load balancer in public subnets in two Availability Zones, and place the application and database instances in private subnets in the same two zones.
- Place the load balancer in public subnets in two Availability Zones, and place the application and database instances in one private subnet that spans both zones.
- Place the load balancer in private subnets in two Availability Zones, and place the application and database instances in public subnets in the same two zones.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Place the load balancer in public subnets in two Availability Zones, and place the application and database instances in private subnets in the same two zones.

**Deciding phrases.** "internet-facing web application", "keep running if one Availability Zone fails", "no direct network path to or from the internet"

**Why.** AWS says to [Distinguish between components that require inbound access from the internet, such as public web endpoints, and those that only need internal access, such as databases](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-wa-sec05-bp01-network-layers). The load balancer is the component that receives traffic from users, so it goes in public subnets. The application and database instances go in private subnets. Subnets in two zones keep the application running when one zone fails.

**Why not.**

- "Place the load balancer, the application instances and ...": A public subnet routes to the internet gateway, so the application and database tiers get a direct path to the internet, which the stem forbids.
- "Place the load balancer in public subnets in ...": Each subnet [must reside entirely within one Availability Zone](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-subnet-single-az) and [cannot span zones](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-subnet-single-az).
- "Place the load balancer in private subnets in ...": The layers are reversed: users on the internet need the load balancer, and the application and database tiers get a direct path to the internet.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the application instances must also download updates from the internet" instead: add a NAT gateway in the public subnets, because a NAT gateway lets private instances start outbound connections.

**Takeaway.** Put the internet-facing load balancer in public subnets and every other tier in private subnets, in two zones.

**Review.** [Every default subnet is public so production tiers belong in private subnets](2-deep.md#every-default-subnet-is-public-so-production-tiers-belong-in-private-subnets-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 4

A company runs a self-managed MySQL database on an Amazon EC2 instance in a private subnet. The application tier runs on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group in two other private subnets. The Auto Scaling group launches and terminates instances many times each day, so the IP addresses of the application instances change often. The database must accept connections on TCP 3306 from the application instances. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST securely?

- Add an inbound rule to the database security group that allows TCP 3306 from the CIDR blocks of the two application subnets.
- Allow TCP 3306 from the application subnets in the network ACL of the database subnet, and allow all inbound traffic in the database security group.
- Add an inbound rule to the database security group that allows TCP 3306 with the security group of the application tier as the source.
- Run a script after each scaling event that adds the private IP address of each new application instance to the database security group.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Add an inbound rule to the database security group that allows TCP 3306 with the security group of the application tier as the source.

**Deciding phrases.** "IP addresses of the application instances change often", "accept connections on TCP 3306 from the application instances", "MOST securely"

**Why.** A security group rule can name another security group as its source, and [the rule affects all instances that are associated with the security groups](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-sg-reference-sg-private-ips). New application instances join the application security group at launch, so the database rule needs no edits when the group scales. AWS uses the same pattern for a database: [Allows inbound MySQL Server access from the web servers](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-sg-chain-db-allows-web-sg).

**Why not.**

- "Add an inbound rule to the database security ...": It works, but any other resource in those two subnets also reaches the database, so the rule is wider than the application tier.
- "Allow TCP 3306 from the application subnets in ...": The security group opens every port to every source, and the network ACL filters by subnet, not by tier, so the database is far less protected.
- "Run a script after each scaling event that ...": It works with effort, but old addresses stay allowed until the script runs; naming the group avoids both, because [the rule affects all instances that are associated with the security groups](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-sg-reference-sg-private-ips).

**Twin.** If the stem said "the database must also block one known hostile address range" instead: add a deny rule in a network ACL, because a security group has [allow rules only](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-sg-vs-nacl-rule-type).

**Takeaway.** When source IP addresses change, name the source security group in the rule instead of addresses.

**Review.** [A security group rule can name another security group as its source](2-deep.md#a-security-group-rule-can-name-another-security-group-as-its-source-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 5

A company runs Amazon EC2 instances in a private subnet. A previous administrator associated an Elastic IP address with each instance, but the instances still cannot download the updates that they need to patch their operating systems. The route table of the private subnet has the local route and no other routes. The VPC also has an internet gateway and a public subnet whose route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to the internet gateway. Which solution will let the instances download the updates MOST securely?

- Add a 0.0.0.0/0 route to the internet gateway in the route table of the private subnet, and keep the Elastic IP addresses on the instances.
- Add an outbound rule that allows HTTPS to 0.0.0.0/0 to the security groups of the instances, and keep the Elastic IP addresses.
- Create a zonal NAT gateway in the private subnet, add a 0.0.0.0/0 route to it in the private route table, and release the Elastic IP addresses.
- Create a NAT gateway in the public subnet, add a 0.0.0.0/0 route to it in the private route table, and release the Elastic IP addresses.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create a NAT gateway in the public subnet, add a 0.0.0.0/0 route to it in the private route table, and release the Elastic IP addresses.

**Deciding phrases.** "Elastic IP address with each instance", "has the local route and no other routes", "MOST securely"

**Why.** To reach the internet from a private subnet, [create a NAT gateway or launch a NAT instance in a public subnet](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-route-from-private-subnet) and send 0.0.0.0/0 to it. The Elastic IP addresses have no use there: they [cannot be used on instances in subnets configured to use a NAT gateway or a NAT instance to access the Internet](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-faq-eip-not-behind-nat), so release them.

**Why not.**

- "Add a 0.0.0.0/0 route to the internet gateway ...": It works, but the subnet becomes public, and the instances can then receive connections from the internet whenever a security group rule allows them.
- "Add an outbound rule that allows HTTPS to ...": The missing piece is a route: [instances in the private subnet can't communicate with the internet, even if they have public IP addresses](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-public-vs-private-subnet-by-igw-route).
- "Create a zonal NAT gateway in the private ...": For internet access, [The NAT gateway must be in a public subnet with a route table that routes internet traffic to an internet gateway](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-troubleshoot-route-placement).

**Twin.** If the stem said "users on the internet must connect to the instances directly" instead: a route to the internet gateway, because [instances in the private subnet can't communicate with the internet, even if they have public IP addresses](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-public-vs-private-subnet-by-igw-route).

**Takeaway.** A private subnet reaches the internet through a NAT gateway (a zonal one sits in a public subnet), not through public IP addresses.

**Review.** [A subnet is public only when its route table points to an internet gateway](2-deep.md#a-subnet-is-public-only-when-its-route-table-points-to-an-internet-gateway-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 6

A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances behind an internet-facing Application Load Balancer. The load balancer and the instances run in the same public subnets, and the instances have public IP addresses. The security groups of the load balancer and of the instances allow HTTPS from 0.0.0.0/0. The security team finds malicious requests that come from one known range of IP addresses. The company must prevent all requests from that range from reaching the application. Which solution will meet this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Change the source of the inbound HTTPS rule in the security group of the instances to the private IP addresses of the load balancer nodes.
- Add an inbound rule that denies the IP address range to the network ACL of the public subnets where the load balancer runs.
- Replace the HTTPS rules for 0.0.0.0/0 in both security groups with allow rules for every address range except the malicious range.
- Change the source of the inbound HTTPS rule in the security group of the instances to the security group of the load balancer.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Add an inbound rule that denies the IP address range to the network ACL of the public subnets where the load balancer runs.

**Deciding phrases.** "prevent all requests from that range", "one known range of IP addresses", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** The requirement is to block one source range. A security group has [allow rules only](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-sg-vs-nacl-rule-type), so it has no way to refuse a range. A network ACL works at the [subnet level](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-sg-vs-nacl-level) and can deny. Rules are evaluated [starting with the lowest numbered rule](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-nacl-rule-order-first-match), so the deny rule gets a lower number than the rule that allows HTTPS.

**Why not.**

- "Change the source of the inbound HTTPS rule ...": The load balancer still accepts the malicious requests and forwards them, so the instances still process requests from that range.
- "Replace the HTTPS rules for 0.0.0.0/0 in both ...": It works, but [you can specify allow rules, but not deny rules](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-sg-allow-rules-only) in a security group, so blocking one range means many allow rules to keep current.
- "Change the source of the inbound HTTPS rule ...": The rule limits the sources that reach the instances, but the malicious range still reaches the load balancer, which forwards the requests.

**Twin.** If the stem said "The company must allow only requests from the load balancer to reach the instances." instead: a rule that [allows inbound HTTPS access from the load balancer](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-sg-chain-web-allows-lb-sg) by its security group.

**Takeaway.** To block a source range, add a deny rule to a network ACL, because a security group has [allow rules only](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-sg-vs-nacl-rule-type).

**Review.** [Security groups remember connections but network ACLs check every packet](2-deep.md#security-groups-remember-connections-but-network-acls-check-every-packet-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=vpc-q009 -->
### Question 7

A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances. All the instances run in one subnet of the company's VPC, and an Application Load Balancer that is enabled in two Availability Zones sends requests to them. Last month, a failure in one Availability Zone stopped the whole application. The company wants the application to be highly available and to keep running if one Availability Zone fails. What should a solutions architect do?

- Change the existing subnet so that it spans a second Availability Zone, and launch more instances in it.
- Replace the instances with larger instance types in the same subnet so that each instance handles more requests.
- Create a subnet in a second Availability Zone, and run instances in both subnets behind the load balancer.
- Create a second VPC in the same Availability Zone, and run a copy of the application in that VPC.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create a subnet in a second Availability Zone, and run instances in both subnets behind the load balancer.

**Deciding phrases.** "All the instances run in one subnet", "keep running if one Availability Zone fails"

**Why.** Each subnet [must reside entirely within one Availability Zone](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-subnet-single-az), so one subnet means one zone. A VPC can hold [one or more subnets in each Availability Zone](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-spans-all-azs-in-region). A second subnet in another zone, with instances in both, removes the single zone from the design.

**Why not.**

- "Change the existing subnet so that it spans ...": A subnet [cannot span zones](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-subnet-single-az), so the existing subnet stays in one Availability Zone.
- "Replace the instances with larger instance types in ...": Larger instances add capacity, but they stay in the same zone, so a failure of that zone still stops the application.
- "Create a second VPC in the same Availability ...": A VPC already [spans all of the Availability Zones in a Region](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-spans-all-azs-in-region), and a second VPC in the same zone adds no new zone.

**Twin.** If the stem said "an outage of one Availability Zone is acceptable for this test copy" instead: keep one subnet, because you can [save money by deploying your resources in only one Availability Zone](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-dev-test-one-az-saves-money).

**Takeaway.** A subnet lives in one Availability Zone, so high availability needs subnets with instances in two or more zones.

**Review.** [A VPC spans every Availability Zone but each subnet lives in one zone](2-deep.md#a-vpc-spans-every-availability-zone-but-each-subnet-lives-in-one-zone-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 8

A company runs an application on Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets in two Availability Zones. The instances download small daily updates from partner websites on the internet. The route tables of both private subnets send 0.0.0.0/0 to one NAT gateway in a public subnet in the first Availability Zone. Outbound internet access must stay highly available during an Availability Zone failure. Which solution is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements?

- Create a NAT gateway in each zone, add a standby NAT gateway next to each one, and route each private subnet to its own zone.
- Keep the one NAT gateway in the first Availability Zone, and keep the routes of both private subnets pointed at that NAT gateway.
- Replace the NAT gateway with an egress-only internet gateway, and route 0.0.0.0/0 from both private subnets to the egress-only internet gateway.
- Create a NAT gateway in a public subnet in the second Availability Zone, and route each private subnet to the NAT gateway in its own zone.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create a NAT gateway in a public subnet in the second Availability Zone, and route each private subnet to the NAT gateway in its own zone.

**Deciding phrases.** "must stay highly available during an Availability Zone failure", "one NAT gateway", "MOST cost-effective"

**Why.** Because [each NAT gateway is created in a specific Availability Zone and implemented with redundancy in that zone](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-one-az-redundant-in-zone), a failure of the first zone stops the shared gateway. One more gateway in the second zone, with a route per zone, removes that dependency at the lowest added cost.

**Why not.**

- "Create a NAT gateway in each zone, add ...": It works, but [each NAT gateway is created in a specific Availability Zone and implemented with redundancy in that zone](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-one-az-redundant-in-zone), so the standby gateways add hourly charges and no availability.
- "Keep the one NAT gateway in the first ...": If the first zone fails, [resources in the other Availability Zones lose internet access](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-shared-across-azs-loses-internet), because the shared NAT gateway is zonal.
- "Replace the NAT gateway with an egress-only internet ...": An egress-only internet gateway is [for use with IPv6 traffic only](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-eigw-ipv6-outbound-only), so the IPv4 traffic of the instances gets no path to the internet.

**Twin.** If the stem said "This is a test environment, and an outage of one Availability Zone is acceptable." instead: keep the one NAT gateway, because each gateway is [charged for each hour that your NAT gateway is available](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-pricing-dimensions).

**Takeaway.** For outbound access that survives a zone failure, create a NAT gateway in each Availability Zone and route each zone to its own.

**Review.** [A zonal NAT gateway fails with its zone but a regional one follows workloads](2-deep.md#a-zonal-nat-gateway-fails-with-its-zone-but-a-regional-one-follows-workloads-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 9

A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances behind an internet-facing Application Load Balancer. The load balancer and the instances run in the same public subnets, and the instances have public IP addresses. The security groups of the load balancer and of the instances allow HTTPS from 0.0.0.0/0. The security team finds malicious requests that come from one known range of IP addresses. The company must allow only requests from the load balancer to reach the instances. Which solution will meet this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Change the source of the inbound HTTPS rule in the security group of the instances to the private IP addresses of the load balancer nodes.
- Add an inbound rule that denies the IP address range to the network ACL of the public subnets where the load balancer runs.
- Replace the HTTPS rules for 0.0.0.0/0 in both security groups with allow rules for every address range except the malicious range.
- Change the source of the inbound HTTPS rule in the security group of the instances to the security group of the load balancer.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Change the source of the inbound HTTPS rule in the security group of the instances to the security group of the load balancer.

**Deciding phrases.** "allow only requests from the load balancer", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** The instances should accept requests from the load balancer alone. A security group rule can take [the ID of a security group](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-sg-rule-sources) as its source, and the example web tier [allows inbound HTTPS access from the load balancer](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-sg-chain-web-allows-lb-sg) this way. After the 0.0.0.0/0 source is replaced, direct requests from the internet match no allow rule.

**Why not.**

- "Change the source of the inbound HTTPS rule ...": Node addresses need updates by hand, while [a security group can have a rule that allows traffic from another security group by its identifier, minimizing updates as resources within the group change over time](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-wa-sec05-bp02-sg-references-sg).
- "Add an inbound rule that denies the IP ...": The deny rule stops one range, but every other address on the internet can still reach the public IP addresses of the instances.
- "Replace the HTTPS rules for 0.0.0.0/0 in both ...": The new rules still let every other address range reach the instances directly, so requests that bypass the load balancer are accepted.

**Twin.** If the stem said "The company must prevent all requests from that range from reaching the application." instead: add a deny rule to the network ACL, because [network ACLs can be used to set both Allow and Deny rules](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-sg-allow-rules-only).

**Takeaway.** To accept traffic from one tier alone, name the security group of that tier as the source of the rule.

**Review.** [A security group rule can name another security group as its source](2-deep.md#a-security-group-rule-can-name-another-security-group-as-its-source-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 10

A company runs an application on Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets in two Availability Zones. The instances download small daily updates from partner websites on the internet. The route tables of both private subnets send 0.0.0.0/0 to one NAT gateway in a public subnet in the first Availability Zone. This is a test environment, and an outage of one Availability Zone is acceptable. Which solution is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements?

- Create a NAT gateway in each zone, add a standby NAT gateway next to each one, and route each private subnet to its own zone.
- Keep the one NAT gateway in the first Availability Zone, and keep the routes of both private subnets pointed at that NAT gateway.
- Replace the NAT gateway with an egress-only internet gateway, and route 0.0.0.0/0 from both private subnets to the egress-only internet gateway.
- Create a NAT gateway in a public subnet in the second Availability Zone, and route each private subnet to the NAT gateway in its own zone.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Keep the one NAT gateway in the first Availability Zone, and keep the routes of both private subnets pointed at that NAT gateway.

**Deciding phrases.** "This is a test environment", "an outage of one Availability Zone is acceptable", "MOST cost-effective"

**Why.** The stem accepts the loss of one zone and asks for the lowest cost. A NAT gateway is [charged for each hour that your NAT gateway is available](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-pricing-dimensions) and for [each gigabyte of data that it processes](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-pricing-dimensions), so every extra gateway adds an hourly charge. The traffic is small, so the existing gateway is the cheapest design that works.

**Why not.**

- "Create a NAT gateway in each zone, add ...": It works, but [each NAT gateway is created in a specific Availability Zone and implemented with redundancy in that zone](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-one-az-redundant-in-zone), so the standbys add cost.
- "Replace the NAT gateway with an egress-only internet ...": An egress-only internet gateway is [for use with IPv6 traffic only](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-eigw-ipv6-outbound-only), so the IPv4 traffic of the instances gets no path to the internet.
- "Create a NAT gateway in a public subnet ...": It works, but a second gateway adds a second hourly charge, because a NAT gateway is [charged for each hour that your NAT gateway is available](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-pricing-dimensions).

**Twin.** If the stem said "Outbound internet access must stay highly available during an Availability Zone failure." instead: add a second NAT gateway, because [resources in the other Availability Zones lose internet access](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-shared-across-azs-loses-internet).

**Takeaway.** In a test environment that accepts a zone outage, one shared NAT gateway is the cheapest working design.

**Review.** [A zonal NAT gateway fails with its zone but a regional one follows workloads](2-deep.md#a-zonal-nat-gateway-fails-with-its-zone-but-a-regional-one-follows-workloads-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

## Extended

<!-- quiz:start id=vpc-q008 -->
### Question 11

A company created a VPC with the CIDR block 10.0.0.0/24 for a pilot project. The project grew, and the VPC now runs an application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group across two subnets. New instances fail to launch because the two subnets have no free IP addresses. The network design must be scalable for the next stage of growth. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Associate a non-overlapping secondary IPv4 CIDR block with the VPC, create new subnets in it, and add them to the Auto Scaling group.
- Change the CIDR block of the VPC from 10.0.0.0/24 to 10.0.0.0/16, and then enlarge the two existing subnets into the new space.
- Create a new VPC with the CIDR block 10.1.0.0/16, migrate the application into new subnets there, and delete the old VPC afterward.
- Associate a secondary IPv4 CIDR block of 10.0.0.0/23 that contains the current block, and launch the new instances in the added addresses.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Associate a non-overlapping secondary IPv4 CIDR block with the VPC, create new subnets in it, and add them to the Auto Scaling group.

**Deciding phrases.** "10.0.0.0/24", "no free IP addresses", "scalable", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** The fix adds address space to the same VPC instead of rebuilding it. You [cannot increase or decrease the size of an existing CIDR block](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-cidr-cannot-resize), so you associate a secondary block that does not overlap the first one. New subnets in that block can route at once, because [a route is automatically added to your VPC route tables to enable routing within the VPC](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-secondary-cidr-adds-local-route).

**Why not.**

- "Change the CIDR block of the VPC from ...": You [cannot increase or decrease the size of an existing CIDR block](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-cidr-cannot-resize), so the VPC block stays a /24.
- "Create a new VPC with the CIDR block ...": It works, but a new VPC and a migration of the whole application is far more work than adding a block to the current VPC.
- "Associate a secondary IPv4 CIDR block of 10.0.0.0/23 ...": A secondary block [must not overlap with any existing CIDR block that's associated with the VPC](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-cidr-cannot-resize), and a /23 that contains 10.0.0.0/24 overlaps it.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the company is still designing the VPC for a product that will grow" instead: choose a large CIDR block now, because Well-Architected warns against [CIDR blocks that are too small and requiring reconfiguration, potentially causing downtime](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-wa-rel02-bp03-subnet-anti-patterns).

**Takeaway.** A full VPC gets a secondary, non-overlapping CIDR block instead of a larger first block.

**Review.** [A VPC CIDR block cannot be resized so plan it for growth](2-deep.md#a-vpc-cidr-block-cannot-be-resized-so-plan-it-for-growth-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=vpc-q014 -->
### Question 12

A company uses NAT instances in public subnets to give Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets outbound access to the internet. The operations team maintains a script that fails over between the NAT instances, and the team must patch the NAT instances every month. Outbound traffic is growing, and the NAT instances are reaching the network bandwidth of their instance type. The private instances start every connection themselves and need no port forwarding. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Move the NAT instances to a larger instance type with more network bandwidth, and keep the failover script and the monthly patching.
- Run the NAT instances in an Auto Scaling group across Availability Zones, and patch them by replacing their AMI every month.
- Replace the NAT instances with an egress-only internet gateway, and add a 0.0.0.0/0 route to it in each private route table.
- Replace the NAT instances with NAT gateways, and update the route tables of the private subnets to send 0.0.0.0/0 to the NAT gateways.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Replace the NAT instances with NAT gateways, and update the route tables of the private subnets to send 0.0.0.0/0 to the NAT gateways.

**Deciding phrases.** "fails over between the NAT instances", "patch the NAT instances every month", "reaching the network bandwidth of their instance type", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** The stem names three burdens: patching, a failover script and bandwidth. AWS states that [NAT gateways provide better availability, higher bandwidth, and requires less administrative effort](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-preferred-over-nat-instance). A NAT gateway is [Managed by AWS](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-vs-instance-maintenance), so no patches and no script remain. The private instances need no port forwarding, so a NAT instance has no feature advantage here.

**Why not.**

- "Move the NAT instances to a larger instance ...": It solves the bandwidth, which [Depends on the bandwidth of the instance type](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-vs-instance-bandwidth), but the team keeps the script and the patching.
- "Run the NAT instances in an Auto Scaling ...": Auto Scaling replaces failed instances, but a NAT instance is still [Managed by you, for example, by installing software updates or operating system patches on the instance](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-vs-instance-maintenance).
- "Replace the NAT instances with an egress-only internet ...": An egress-only internet gateway is [for use with IPv6 traffic only](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-eigw-ipv6-outbound-only), so it does not carry this IPv4 traffic.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the same device must also forward an inbound port to one private instance" instead: keep a NAT instance, because for a NAT gateway port forwarding is [Not supported](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-vs-instance-port-forwarding).

**Takeaway.** Prefer a NAT gateway to a NAT instance unless the design needs port forwarding.

**Review.** [A zonal NAT gateway fails with its zone but a regional one follows workloads](2-deep.md#a-zonal-nat-gateway-fails-with-its-zone-but-a-regional-one-follows-workloads-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=vpc-q016 -->
### Question 13

A company runs dual-stack Amazon EC2 instances in a private subnet of a VPC that has an IPv6 CIDR block. The instances must download updates from servers on the internet that are reachable over IPv6 addresses. The network path must prevent the internet from starting connections to the instances, whatever their security groups allow. The VPC already has an internet gateway for its public subnets. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Create an egress-only internet gateway, and add a route for ::/0 with the egress-only internet gateway as its target to the private route table.
- Add a route for ::/0 with the existing internet gateway as its target to the route table of the private subnet of the instances.
- Create an egress-only internet gateway, and add a route for 0.0.0.0/0 with the egress-only internet gateway as its target to the private route table.
- Launch a fleet of proxy instances in a public subnet, and route ::/0 from the private subnet to the proxies, which forward the update requests.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create an egress-only internet gateway, and add a route for ::/0 with the egress-only internet gateway as its target to the private route table.

**Deciding phrases.** "reachable over IPv6 addresses", "prevent the internet from starting connections to the instances", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** An egress-only internet gateway [allows outbound communication over IPv6 from instances in your VPC to the internet, and prevents the internet from initiating an IPv6 connection with your instances](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-eigw-ipv6-outbound-only). The gateway is a VPC component, so the team runs no servers for it. The route for ::/0 sends every IPv6 destination on the internet to the gateway.

**Why not.**

- "Add a route for ::/0 with the existing ...": The route makes the subnet public for IPv6, and [IPv6 addresses are globally unique, and therefore public by default](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-eip-ipv6-not-supported), so the internet can start connections.
- "Create an egress-only internet gateway, and add a ...": The gateway is [for use with IPv6 traffic only](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-eigw-ipv6-outbound-only), and the updates go to IPv6 addresses, which a 0.0.0.0/0 route does not match.
- "Launch a fleet of proxy instances in a ...": It can work, but the team runs, patches and scales a proxy fleet, which is far more work than one managed gateway and one route.

**Twin.** If the stem said "servers that are reachable over IPv4 addresses" instead: a NAT gateway, because AWS says [To enable outbound-only internet communication over IPv4, use a NAT gateway instead](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-eigw-ipv6-outbound-only).

**Takeaway.** Outbound-only IPv6 uses an egress-only internet gateway; outbound-only IPv4 uses a NAT gateway.

**Review.** [IPv6 addresses are public so outbound-only IPv6 uses an egress-only internet gateway](2-deep.md#ipv6-addresses-are-public-so-outbound-only-ipv6-uses-an-egress-only-internet-gateway-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=vpc-q011 -->
### Question 14

A company runs Amazon EC2 instances in a public subnet. The route table of the subnet sends 0.0.0.0/0 to an internet gateway. The instances upload files to an Amazon S3 bucket in the same AWS Region and download reports from a partner website on the internet. A new security rule requires that the S3 uploads travel privately and do not use the internet gateway. Access to the partner website must continue. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Create an interface endpoint for Amazon S3 in the subnet, and change the application to send uploads to the DNS name of the endpoint.
- Create a gateway endpoint for Amazon S3, associate it with the route table of the subnet, and keep the 0.0.0.0/0 route to the internet gateway.
- Create a gateway endpoint for Amazon S3, associate it with the route table of the subnet, and delete the 0.0.0.0/0 route to the internet gateway.
- Move the instances to a private subnet, and send all their outbound traffic, including the S3 uploads, through a NAT gateway in the public subnet.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create a gateway endpoint for Amazon S3, associate it with the route table of the subnet, and keep the 0.0.0.0/0 route to the internet gateway.

**Deciding phrases.** "S3 uploads travel privately", "Access to the partner website must continue", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** A gateway endpoint adds a route whose destination is the S3 prefix list, and the route table uses [longest prefix match](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-route-longest-prefix-match), not the order of the routes. So [the endpoint route takes precedence for traffic destined for the service (Amazon S3 or DynamoDB) in the current Region](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-gateway-endpoint-beats-igw-default-route), and other internet traffic still uses 0.0.0.0/0.

**Why not.**

- "Create an interface endpoint for Amazon S3 in ...": It works, but it adds an application change and charges, because an interface endpoint is [billed for each hour that your interface VPC endpoint is provisioned in each Availability Zone](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-interface-endpoint-billed-hour-per-az-and-gb).
- "Create a gateway endpoint for Amazon S3, associate ...": Deleting the default route stops the website downloads, and route order does not matter, because the route table uses [longest prefix match](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-route-longest-prefix-match).
- "Move the instances to a private subnet, and ...": The uploads still reach the internet gateway, because [the NAT gateway must be in a public subnet with a route table that routes internet traffic to an internet gateway](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-troubleshoot-route-placement).

**Twin.** If the stem said "an S3 bucket in another AWS Region" instead: those uploads keep using the internet gateway, because [prefix lists are specific to a Region](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-gateway-endpoint-beats-igw-default-route).

**Takeaway.** A gateway endpoint route beats the 0.0.0.0/0 route for S3 in the same Region, because the most specific route wins.

**Review.** [A route table sends subnet traffic and the most specific route wins](2-deep.md#a-route-table-sends-subnet-traffic-and-the-most-specific-route-wins-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=vpc-q019 -->
### Question 15

A company has a hybrid architecture. Servers in the company's on-premises data center connect to a VPC over an existing AWS Direct Connect connection that ends at a virtual private gateway. The servers must upload backup files to an Amazon S3 bucket in the same AWS Region as the VPC. The uploads must travel privately and must not use the public internet. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Create a gateway endpoint for Amazon S3, and associate it with the route table of the subnets that the Direct Connect traffic enters.
- Launch proxy instances in the VPC that receive the uploads from the data center and write them to Amazon S3 through a gateway endpoint.
- Create an interface endpoint for Amazon S3 in the VPC, and configure the servers to send uploads to the DNS name of the endpoint.
- Create a NAT gateway in a public subnet of the VPC, and route the uploads from the data center through the virtual private gateway to it.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create an interface endpoint for Amazon S3 in the VPC, and configure the servers to send uploads to the DNS name of the endpoint.

**Deciding phrases.** "on-premises data center", "Direct Connect connection that ends at a virtual private gateway", "travel privately", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** The traffic starts outside the VPC, and [gateway endpoints do not allow access from on-premises networks, from peered VPCs in other AWS Regions, or through a transit gateway](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-gateway-endpoint-no-onprem-cross-region-tgw). For those cases [you must use an interface endpoint, which is available for an additional cost](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-gateway-endpoint-no-onprem-cross-region-tgw). The interface endpoint has private IP addresses in the VPC, so the Direct Connect path reaches it.

**Why not.**

- "Create a gateway endpoint for Amazon S3, and ...": The data center cannot use it, because [gateway endpoints do not allow access from on-premises networks, from peered VPCs in other AWS Regions, or through a transit gateway](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-gateway-endpoint-no-onprem-cross-region-tgw).
- "Launch proxy instances in the VPC that receive ...": It works, but the proxy instances add instances to patch, scale and keep available, which a managed endpoint avoids.
- "Create a NAT gateway in a public subnet ...": The route fails, because you [can't route traffic to a NAT gateway from Site-to-Site VPN or Direct Connect using a virtual private gateway](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-not-via-peering-or-vgw), and a NAT gateway leads to the internet.

**Twin.** If the stem said "Amazon EC2 instances in the VPC" instead: a gateway endpoint, because [there are no data processing or hourly charges for using Gateway Type VPC endpoints](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-gateway-endpoint-no-hourly-or-processing-charge).

**Takeaway.** Traffic from on premises reaches Amazon S3 privately through an interface endpoint, not through a gateway endpoint.

**Review.** [AWS service endpoints are public but a VPC endpoint reaches them privately](2-deep.md#aws-service-endpoints-are-public-but-a-vpc-endpoint-reaches-them-privately-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=vpc-q013 -->
### Question 16

A company runs batch workers on Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets in three Availability Zones. The route tables of all private subnets send 0.0.0.0/0 to one NAT gateway in the first Availability Zone. Most of the traffic of the workers goes to Amazon S3 buckets in the same AWS Region, and the workers also download a significant volume of data from software repositories on the internet. The workers must stay in private subnets in all three zones. The bill shows high NAT gateway data processing charges and charges for data transfer between Availability Zones. Which combination of steps is the MOST cost-effective way to reduce these charges? (Select TWO.)

- Move the workers to public subnets, give each worker a public IPv4 address, and delete the NAT gateway in the first Availability Zone.
- Associate a second Elastic IP address with the existing NAT gateway so that it can process the traffic of all three zones.
- Create a gateway endpoint for Amazon S3, and associate it with the route tables of all the private subnets.
- Create an interface endpoint for Amazon S3 in each Availability Zone, and send the S3 traffic of the workers to the endpoint network interfaces.
- Create a NAT gateway in each Availability Zone that has workers, and route each private subnet to the NAT gateway in its own zone.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.**

- Create a gateway endpoint for Amazon S3, and associate it with the route tables of all the private subnets.
- Create a NAT gateway in each Availability Zone that has workers, and route each private subnet to the NAT gateway in its own zone.

**Deciding phrases.** "Amazon S3 buckets in the same AWS Region", "charges for data transfer between Availability Zones", "must stay in private subnets", "MOST cost-effective"

**Why.** S3 in the same Region looks free, but NAT gateway data processing applies [regardless of the traffic's source or destination](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-data-processing-any-destination). A gateway endpoint takes the S3 bytes off the NAT gateway. A NAT gateway in each zone ends the cross-zone transfer for the internet downloads.

- [There are no data processing or hourly charges for using Gateway Type VPC endpoints](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-gateway-endpoint-no-hourly-or-processing-charge), so the S3 traffic leaves the NAT gateway.
- For a significant volume across zones, the advice is to [create a NAT gateway in each Availability Zone with resources](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-same-az-reduces-charges), which ends the cross-zone transfer.

**Why not.**

- "Move the workers to public subnets, give each ...": The workers must stay in private subnets, and [you pay an hourly rate for each public IPv4 address used by your AWS account](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-public-ipv4-hourly-in-use-or-idle).
- "Associate a second Elastic IP address with the ...": Each address adds room for [55,000 simultaneous connections](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-nat-55000-connections-per-ip) to each unique destination, but the per-gigabyte and cross-zone charges stay the same.
- "Create an interface endpoint for Amazon S3 in ...": It works, but for an interface endpoint [you are also billed per GB of data processed](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-interface-endpoint-billed-hour-per-az-and-gb), unlike a gateway endpoint.

**Twin.** If the stem said "Amazon DynamoDB tables" instead: create a gateway endpoint for DynamoDB, because [Gateway VPC endpoints provide reliable connectivity to Amazon S3 and DynamoDB without requiring an internet gateway or a NAT device for your VPC](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-gateway-endpoint-s3-dynamodb-no-privatelink).

**Takeaway.** Cut NAT gateway bills with a gateway endpoint for S3 traffic and a NAT gateway in each zone for internet traffic.

**Review.** [Data transfer is free inside one Availability Zone but charged across zones](2-deep.md#data-transfer-is-free-inside-one-availability-zone-but-charged-across-zones-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=vpc-q015 -->
### Question 17

A company runs workloads on Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets of one VPC. Auto Scaling groups add and remove instances in three Availability Zones, and some zones have no instances for weeks. The instances need outbound IPv4 internet access that is highly available. The network team does not want to create and track a NAT gateway, a public subnet and a separate route for each Availability Zone. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Create one zonal NAT gateway in a public subnet in the first Availability Zone, and point the 0.0.0.0/0 route of every private subnet to it.
- Create one regional NAT gateway in manual mode, and add or remove its Availability Zones whenever the Auto Scaling groups change zones.
- Create a private NAT gateway in each Availability Zone, and point the 0.0.0.0/0 route of each private subnet to the gateway in its zone.
- Create one regional NAT gateway in automatic mode, and point the 0.0.0.0/0 route of every private subnet to the regional NAT gateway.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create one regional NAT gateway in automatic mode, and point the 0.0.0.0/0 route of every private subnet to the regional NAT gateway.

**Deciding phrases.** "some zones have no instances for weeks", "outbound IPv4 internet access that is highly available", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** The workloads move between zones, and the team wants no gateway or route for each zone. A regional NAT gateway has two modes. In automatic mode [AWS automatically manages IP addresses and Availability Zone expansion](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-regional-nat-modes), but in manual mode [you are responsible for expanding and contracting your NAT gateway across Availability Zones](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-regional-nat-modes). Automatic mode leaves the team one gateway to manage.

**Why not.**

- "Create one zonal NAT gateway in a public ...": The gateway is zonal, so if the first zone fails, [resources in the other Availability Zones lose internet access](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-shared-across-azs-loses-internet).
- "Create one regional NAT gateway in manual mode, ...": It works, but in manual mode [you are responsible for expanding and contracting your NAT gateway across Availability Zones](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-regional-nat-modes).
- "Create a private NAT gateway in each Availability ...": A private NAT gateway sends traffic [to other VPCs or on-premises networks using Transit Gateway or a virtual private gateway](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-private-connectivity-type), not to the internet.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the instances must reach other VPCs through a transit gateway, not the internet" instead: use a zonal private NAT gateway, because regional NAT gateways [do not support private NAT](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-regional-nat-no-private-nat).

**Takeaway.** When workloads move between zones, a regional NAT gateway in automatic mode gives highly available outbound access with one route target.

**Review.** [A zonal NAT gateway fails with its zone but a regional one follows workloads](2-deep.md#a-zonal-nat-gateway-fails-with-its-zone-but-a-regional-one-follows-workloads-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=vpc-q021 -->
### Question 18

A company runs worker instances in one private subnet. The workers process jobs from a queue and download data from the internet through a NAT gateway in a public subnet. All the subnets and the NAT gateway are in the same Availability Zone. The company wants the workers to be fault tolerant and to keep processing jobs if that Availability Zone fails. Which combination of steps is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

- Create a private subnet in a second Availability Zone, and run worker instances in both private subnets.
- Change the existing private subnet so that it spans a second Availability Zone, and launch more workers in it.
- Associate a second Elastic IP address with the existing NAT gateway so that the NAT gateway keeps working if its zone fails.
- Create a NAT gateway in a public subnet in the second zone, and route each private subnet to the NAT gateway in its zone.
- Create a NAT gateway in every Availability Zone of the Region, including the zones that have no worker instances.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.**

- Create a private subnet in a second Availability Zone, and run worker instances in both private subnets.
- Create a NAT gateway in a public subnet in the second zone, and route each private subnet to the NAT gateway in its zone.

**Deciding phrases.** "All the subnets and the NAT gateway are in the same Availability Zone", "fault tolerant", "MOST cost-effective"

**Why.** The design has two single points of failure in one zone, the subnet with the workers and the NAT gateway. A design principle is to [avoid single points of failure, including the underlying physical infrastructure](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-wa-rel10-bp01-avoid-single-points-of-failure). Workers in a second zone and a NAT gateway in that zone remove both, at the cost of one more gateway.

- Resources in separate zones [protect your applications from the failure of a single Availability Zone](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-subnet-one-az-protects-from-zone-failure), so the workers no longer depend on one zone.
- The advice is to [create a NAT gateway in each Availability Zone, and configure your routing to ensure that resources use the NAT gateway in the same Availability Zone](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-shared-across-azs-loses-internet).

**Why not.**

- "Change the existing private subnet so that it ...": A subnet [cannot span zones](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-subnet-single-az), so the subnet stays in the zone that can fail.
- "Associate a second Elastic IP address with the ...": Extra addresses add connections, but [each NAT gateway is created in a specific Availability Zone and implemented with redundancy in that zone](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-one-az-redundant-in-zone).
- "Create a NAT gateway in every Availability Zone ...": It works, but every NAT gateway is [charged for each hour that your NAT gateway is available](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-pricing-dimensions), and zones without workers need no gateway.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the workers download nothing from the internet" instead: the second subnet with workers is enough, and the second zone needs no NAT gateway.

**Takeaway.** Remove each single point of failure: subnets with instances in two zones, and a NAT gateway in each zone that has instances.

**Review.** [A VPC spans every Availability Zone but each subnet lives in one zone](2-deep.md#a-vpc-spans-every-availability-zone-but-each-subnet-lives-in-one-zone-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->
